assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and credit cycles are a foundational mechanism for how small shocks are amplified and propagated. The work reshaped macroeconomics, financial-crisis analysis and policy thinking, and it sits in the core of modern dynamic general-equilibrium modelling.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is the clearest anchor for the collateral-constraint mechanism. Gertler is credited for the financial-accelerator and macro-financial strand developed with Bernanke and others. Bernanke and Gilchrist have claims on the accelerator, and Bernanke's prior recognition in 2022 limits the room for that strand. I therefore centre the award on the collateral-constraint and credit-cycle contribution.
assessment.maturity: Foundational papers date from the 1990s. Their value has been tested over decades, and the 2008 crisis and later empirical and quantitative work strongly confirmed the relevance. Timing is not an obstacle.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises could make the committee see the area as already honoured.
The division of credit between the collateral-constraint and financial-accelerator strands is contestable.
Whether Gertler or Gilchrist belongs in the trio depends on how the citation is framed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection transformed international trade theory and empirics. They changed how the gains from trade, reallocation and productivity are understood, and they are now the standard workhorse framework.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman is a long-standing leader in the theory and in the empirical firm-level trade literature. Redding has major contributions to quantitative and spatial extensions but is arguably later and more derivative of the core insight. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not listed here and may merit consideration.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across many datasets and countries, with wide adoption in textbooks and policy analysis.
uncertainties: The longlist omits some contributors to the heterogeneous-firm trade literature, so the credit may be incomplete.
Helpman also appears in a separate trade political-economy candidate, so the committee must avoid overlap and decide where his credit sits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formal, empirically grounded analysis of how political institutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. It created a coherent field of modern political economics, and it is highly relevant to policy-making and institutional design.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central figures through their theory and empirical work on constitutions and electoral rules. Besley is closely linked, especially on state capacity and accountability. The three are plausibly a natural trio. Some members may have personal or institutional proximity to these candidates, which I disclose and do not adjudicate.
assessment.maturity: The core contributions date from the 1990s and 2000s and have been extended and confirmed by a large literature. Some identification questions remain open.
uncertainties: Causal identification of constitutional effects is debated.
The committee might prefer a different pairing, or the work of Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson on institutions, which won in 2024, might be seen as covering overlapping ground.
Possible personal or institutional proximity of committee members to the candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rubinstein's alternating-offers model is the canonical non-cooperative bargaining theory, and the market-bargaining extensions with Wolinsky broadened its reach. The work is foundational for labour, search and matching, and contract theory.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the core contribution. Wolinsky co-authored the key work on bargaining in decentralised markets. Binmore contributed to the strategic foundations and interpretation, but a smaller prize group seems more defensible, and Stahl's independent contribution on the finite-horizon version is also relevant.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. More than 40 years of use across fields.
uncertainties: The game-theory fields have been heavily recognised in recent decades, which might lower priority.
Attribution relative to Stahl and Binmore is a matter of judgment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference and heterogeneous treatment effects, including double/debiased ML and causal forests, have changed applied empirical practice across fields. They extend the credibility revolution recognised in 2021.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov is a central figure through debiased ML and high-dimensional inference. Athey is a central figure through causal trees and forests and applied policy-learning work. Wager is a key co-developer of the forest methods but is more junior. Imbens's prior recognition and the ties to Wager's and others' work complicate the credit.
assessment.maturity: The methods are widely adopted but relatively recent, with ongoing development. Long-run durability is less proven than for the older candidates.
uncertainties: It is uncertain whether the field is mature enough or whether the contributions will be judged as extensions of prior Nobel-recognised work.
Credit is shared with many co-authors, such as Newey, Hansen and Robins, who are not listed here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Resource misallocation across firms is a quantitatively important explanation of cross-country income differences. It links micro-level distortions to aggregate productivity and growth, and it bears on policy for development and growth.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the key paper, and their joint body of work on misallocation and on the Chinese and Indian economies is central. Restuccia and Rogerson developed closely related ideas independently, so attribution is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Substantial in citations and adoption, but measurement of misallocation and the interpretation of wedges remain debated.
uncertainties: Attribution across Restuccia, Rogerson and others.
Measurement concerns about whether estimated wedges reflect true distortions or measurement error.
Overlap with recent growth-related prizes (2018, 2025).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run, administrative-data-based measurement of top income and wealth shares changed the empirical and public understanding of inequality. It opened a major research programme and had broad policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez established the top-income series (with Atkinson, deceased). Zucman's wealth and offshore-wealth work is a more recent extension. The pairing of Piketty and Saez is most defensible on the measurement contribution.
assessment.maturity: The measurement work is mature and widely used, but interpretation of causes and of the wealth-tax and r>g arguments remains contested, and some measurement choices are disputed.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the distributional accounts and of the wealth estimates.
The committee may weigh the political prominence of the work against its scientific contribution; this should not matter, but it may affect how the work is received.
Atkinson's death limits the candidate group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large-scale administrative data have given new measures of intergenerational mobility and of neighbourhood effects, with policy-relevant findings. The work shows great methodological innovation and impact on the empirical study of opportunity.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure of the programme, with Hendren a key co-author on neighbourhood and causal-place effects. Friedman and Katz are credited too. The programme is highly collaborative, and attributing it to a small number of people is hard. I note a topical affinity with my own early research on social mobility, which I disclose.
assessment.maturity: Relatively recent, with many results from the 2010s onward. Replication and long-run durability are still developing, so this ranks below more established candidates.
uncertainties: Maturity and the long-run confirmation of the findings.
Collaborative attribution across a large group of researchers.
Chetty also appears in the optimal-taxation candidate, so credit overlaps.
